exposure.port.21: FTP: file transfer with unencrypted passwords; rarely needed at home.
exposure.port.22: SSH: remote command line. Fine on a NAS or computer you manage - make sure the password is strong.
exposure.port.23: Telnet: unencrypted remote login, a favorite of IoT botnets such as Mirai. Turn it off if you can, or isolate the device.
exposure.port.80: HTTP: a web/admin page without encryption. Normal for routers and printers; change its default password.
exposure.port.443: HTTPS: an encrypted web/admin page. Usually fine.
exposure.port.445: SMB: Windows file sharing. Expected only on PCs and NAS boxes; keep them updated.
exposure.port.554: RTSP: a camera's video stream. Anyone on your network may be able to watch it - check that it needs a password.
exposure.port.1883: MQTT: smart-home messaging without encryption. Fine on a home-automation hub, unexpected elsewhere.
exposure.port.3389: RDP: Windows Remote Desktop, a frequent target of attacks. Keep it off unless you use it.
exposure.port.5555: ADB: Android debugging over the network - full control of the device without a password. Turn it off.
exposure.port.7547: TR-069: ISP remote management, exploited at scale in the past. Unexpected on anything but the ISP's modem.
exposure.port.8080: HTTP (alternate port): often a device's admin or setup page.
exposure.port.8443: HTTPS (alternate port): often a device's encrypted admin page.
exposure.port.9100: Raw printing (JetDirect): anyone on your network can print. Normal for printers.

fam.note: These are estimates from DNS lookups, meant to start a family conversation — not to watch over anyone. Talk about it together, and respect every household member's privacy, especially teenagers'.
fam.method: How it is estimated: lookups of apps such as YouTube or Roblox are grouped into sessions (a pause of up to 5–15 minutes, depending on the kind of app, still counts). Background traffic — clock, updates, phone-home, ads and trackers, unknown sites — never counts, and a device gets at most 60 minutes per hour. DNS caching, VPNs, encrypted DNS or mobile data hide some use; a shared device such as the TV is not one person.

sug.port.title: Close {service} (port {port}) on {name}
sug.port.why: {name} ({ip}) accepts connections on port {port} ({service}). Anyone on your network - including a hacked gadget - can try to log in there.
sug.port.steps.device:
Open the device's app or its web page (http://{ip}) and look for a setting such as Remote access, Telnet, SSH or File sharing.
Turn off the service you do not use, then restart the device.
Check its ports again from the device page in netwarden.
sug.port.steps.router:
If you cannot turn it off, move the device to the router's guest or IoT network so other devices cannot reach it.
Make sure the router does not forward port {port} to {ip} (Port forwarding / Virtual server).
sug.upnp.title: Remove the router forward {proto} {ext} → {name}
sug.upnp.why: Your router lets the internet reach {name} ({ip}:{port}, {service}) on {proto} port {ext}, because the device asked for it via UPnP. Anyone on the internet can try that service.
sug.upnp.steps.router:
Open the router's admin page and find UPnP (often under Advanced or NAT).
Turn UPnP off, or delete the mapping for port {ext} if the router lists them.
Restart the router; netwarden sees on its next check that the forward is gone.
sug.upnp.steps.device:
In the device's app, turn off remote or cloud access features you do not use (they ask for the forward).
Update the device's firmware.
sug.threat.title: Block the dangerous domains {name} contacts
sug.threat.why: {name} looked up {domains}, which are on a list of malicious or high-risk domains. Blocking them stops the connection while you find out why.
sug.threat.steps.adguard:
Open AdGuard Home → Filters → Custom filtering rules.
Paste the rules below and click Apply.
sug.threat.steps.pihole:
Open Pi-hole → Domains.
Add each name below as an exact deny entry.
sug.threat.steps.device:
Update or reset the device, remove apps you do not recognize and change the passwords used on it.
If it keeps contacting these domains, keep it off your network.
sug.doh.title: Stop {name} from bypassing your DNS filter
sug.doh.why: {name} uses its own encrypted DNS resolver ({resolvers}), so its lookups skip AdGuard Home / Pi-hole: nothing is blocked and netwarden cannot see them.
sug.doh.steps.adguard:
Open AdGuard Home → Filters → Custom filtering rules.
Paste the rules below (they block the encrypted resolver's names) and click Apply.
sug.doh.steps.pihole:
Open Pi-hole → Domains.
Add the names below as exact deny entries.
sug.doh.steps.device: On the device, turn off Private DNS / Secure DNS / DNS over HTTPS (Android: Settings → Network → Private DNS → Off; browsers: Settings → Privacy → Secure DNS).
sug.trackers.title: Block {n} trackers that still get through
sug.trackers.why: Your home's tracker grade is {grade}: only {pct}% of tracker lookups were blocked in the last 24 hours. Blocking them stops advertising and analytics companies from following your devices.
sug.trackers.done: The tracker rules you added are working
sug.trackers.steps.adguard:
Open AdGuard Home → Filters → Custom filtering rules.
Paste the rules below and click Apply.
If an app stops working, remove its line again.
sug.trackers.steps.pihole:
Open Pi-hole → Domains.
Add the names below as exact deny entries.
If an app stops working, remove its entry again.
sug.blocklist.title: Turn on a tracker blocklist
sug.blocklist.why: Your home's tracker grade is {grade} and only {pct}% of tracker lookups are blocked. A maintained blocklist covers thousands of trackers at once.
sug.blocklist.done: A blocklist is catching trackers now
sug.blocklist.steps.adguard:
Open AdGuard Home → Filters → DNS blocklists → Add blocklist → Choose from the list.
Tick a privacy list such as AdGuard DNS filter and save.
sug.blocklist.steps.pihole:
Open Pi-hole → Lists and add the address of a privacy blocklist you trust.
Then run Tools → Update Gravity.
sug.ai_redact.title: Turn on redaction for the cloud AI
sug.ai_redact.why: netwarden sends network summaries to a cloud AI ({provider}) with redaction off, so device names, owners and addresses leave your home as they are.
sug.ai_redact.done: Redaction is on for the cloud AI
sug.ai_redact.steps.netwarden:
Open Settings → AI.
Set Redaction to Auto or On and save.
Use "Preview what will be sent" to check the result.
sug.outages_isp.title: Report the repeated internet outages to your provider
sug.outages_isp.why: Your internet dropped {n} times in the last 7 days ({minutes} min in total) while your router kept answering, so the problem is most likely on the provider's side.
sug.outages_isp.steps.isp:
Contact your internet provider and give them the outage times below (copy them).
Ask them to check the line and the modem's signal.
sug.outages_isp.steps.router:
Restart the modem / router once and check its cables.

sug.outages_router.title: Check your router: it stopped answering {n} times
sug.outages_router.why: Your router did not answer at all {n} times in the last 7 days ({minutes} min in total). That points to the router or the Wi-Fi link, not the internet provider.
sug.outages_router.steps.router:
Make sure the router is not overheating and has room around it.
Install the latest router firmware and restart it.
If this computer uses Wi-Fi, try a cable to rule out Wi-Fi drops.

hyg.upnp.title: UPnP on the router
hyg.upnp.unknown: netwarden has not looked for UPnP yet (it does at the next LAN discovery).

hyg.upnp.steps:
Open the router's admin page and find UPnP (often under Advanced or NAT).
If nothing you use needs it (some game consoles do), turn it off.
If you keep it on, look at the list of forwards now and then.

hyg.upnp_risky.fail: {n} forward(s) expose a risky service to the internet: {ports}.
hyg.upnp_risky.steps:
Remove these forwards on the router's UPnP or port-forwarding page.
In the device's app, turn off remote access you do not use.
Update the device's firmware.
hyg.upnp_stale.title: Forwards to devices that are gone
hyg.upnp_stale.pass: Every forward points at a device that is still here.
hyg.upnp_stale.warn: {n} forward(s) point at an address no current device holds: {ports}. Another device could get that address later.
hyg.upnp_stale.steps:
Delete these forwards on the router.
Restarting the router clears most UPnP forwards.
hyg.router.title: Router model and firmware
hyg.router.unknown: The router did not announce its model. The label on the router shows it.
hyg.router.pass: Your router announces itself as {model}. netwarden cannot see its firmware version.
hyg.router.steps:
Search for “{model} firmware” on the maker's support website (type its address yourself).
Compare it with the version on the router's status page and update if a newer one exists.
If the maker no longer publishes updates, consider replacing the router.
hyg.dns_bypass.title: Devices bypassing the DNS filter
hyg.dns_bypass.pass: Every device uses the network's DNS.
hyg.dns_bypass.warn: {n} device(s) use their own encrypted DNS: {names}. netwarden and the filter cannot see their lookups.
hyg.dns_bypass.steps:
Turn off “secure DNS” / “private DNS” on these devices or in their browsers.
Or block the encrypted-DNS providers in AdGuard Home / Pi-hole (see the suggestion).
hyg.exposure.title: Risky open services
hyg.exposure.unknown: No port check yet. Run one from a device's page (opt-in, local network only).
hyg.exposure.pass: The last port check found no risky open service.
hyg.exposure.steps:
Turn off the services you do not use (Telnet, file sharing, remote desktop).
Keep the ones you need behind a strong password and up to date.
hyg.iot.title: Smart-home devices and trackers
hyg.iot.pass: No smart-home device has heavy tracker contact.
hyg.iot.warn: {n} smart-home device(s) talk to trackers a lot: {names}.
hyg.iot.steps:
Put smart-home devices on a guest or IoT network (most routers offer a guest Wi-Fi).
Then they cannot reach your computers and phones.
Block their tracker domains in AdGuard Home / Pi-hole.

sug.upnp_stale.why: {n} router forward(s) point at addresses no current device holds ({ports}). If another device gets one of these addresses, the internet can reach it.
sug.upnp_stale.done: No router forward points at a missing device
sug.upnp_stale.steps.router:
Open the router's admin page and find UPnP or port forwarding.
Delete the forwards listed above, or restart the router (UPnP forwards are usually cleared).
netwarden sees on its next check that they are gone.

push.help.ntfy: ntfy delivers to the ntfy app on your phone. Use your own ntfy server or ntfy.sh; anyone who knows a public topic name can read it, so pick a long random topic or use an access token.
push.help.gotify: Gotify is a self-hosted push server. In Gotify, create an application and paste its app token here.
push.help.homeassistant: Calls a Home Assistant notify service (for example the companion app on your phone). Create a long-lived access token in your Home Assistant profile; list the notify services with the button below.
push.help.webhook: Posts a small JSON document (schema netwarden.notification/1) to any URL, e.g. n8n or Node-RED. With a shared secret, every request carries an HMAC-SHA256 signature header.
push.help.discord: In Discord: Server settings > Integrations > Webhooks > New webhook, then copy the webhook URL. The URL itself is the password: keep it private.
push.help.slack: Create a Slack app with an incoming webhook for one channel and paste the webhook URL. The URL itself is the password: keep it private.
push.help.telegram: Create a bot with @BotFather and paste its token. Then send your bot any message and press "Find my chat id" to fill in the chat id.
push.help.line: LINE Notify ended in 2025; this uses the LINE Messaging API. Create a Messaging API channel for a LINE Official Account, issue a channel access token and enter your user id (U...) or a group id. Push messages count against the account's monthly free quota.
push.help.matrix: Sends a plain-text notice to a Matrix room. Use a dedicated bot account: its access token and the room id (!...:server) the bot has joined.
push.level_help.minimal: Only that something happened and its category - no names, no addresses: "1 new alert: Security. Open the dashboard for details."
push.level_help.standard: A plain-language sentence with device names, like on the dashboard. Never MAC or IP addresses and never the domains a device visited.
push.level_help.detailed: Adds IP and MAC addresses and the domain behind a threat alert. For a channel outside your own network you have to confirm this.

push.err.config: The channel is not set up completely. Edit it and fill in the missing fields.
push.err.http_400: The service rejected the message (400). Check the topic, chat, room or user id.
push.err.http_401: The service did not accept the token or password (401). Create a new one and save it again.
push.err.http_403: The service refused access (403). Check that the token may post to this topic, channel or room.
push.err.http_404: The address was not found (404). The webhook may have been deleted or the URL is mistyped.
push.err.http_429: The service asks us to slow down (429). netwarden waits and tries again; lower the messages per hour if it keeps happening.
push.err.http_4xx: The service rejected the request. Check the channel settings against the service's setup guide.
push.err.http_5xx: The service had a problem on its side. netwarden tries again a few times.
push.err.redirect: The server answered with a redirect, which netwarden never follows. Enter the final address (often https:// instead of http://).
push.err.timeout: The service did not answer in time. Check that it is reachable from this computer; netwarden tries again.
push.err.connect: Could not connect to the server. Check the address and port and that the server is running.
push.err.dns: The server name could not be found. Check the spelling of the address.
push.err.tls: The server's certificate could not be verified. For a self-hosted server with a self-signed certificate, enter its SHA-256 fingerprint as the pinned certificate.
push.err.tls_pin: The server's certificate does not match the pinned fingerprint. If you renewed the certificate, enter the new fingerprint; otherwise something is in between.
push.err.too_large: The message was too large to send.
push.err.bad_answer: The service answered something netwarden did not understand. Check the address.
err.push_url: Enter an http:// or https:// address without user name, password, query or #.
err.push_pin: A certificate fingerprint is 64 hexadecimal digits (SHA-256), with or without colons.
err.push_pin_http: A pinned certificate only applies to https:// addresses.
err.push_webhook_discord: That is not a Discord webhook URL (https://discord.com/api/webhooks/...).
err.push_webhook_slack: That is not a Slack incoming-webhook URL (https://hooks.slack.com/services/...).
err.push_telegram_token: A Telegram bot token looks like 123456789:ABC... (from @BotFather).
err.push_reenter: The address changed: enter this secret again (a saved one is never sent to a new server).
err.push_invalid: This value is not valid here.
err.push_unknown: There is no such notification channel.
